title: Plastic Repairs: Know the Material First
introduction:
“Plastic” is a family name, not a repair recipe. Similar-looking Mustang trim can need different preparation, bonding materials and repair methods. I check the vehicle’s actual trim and finish before deciding whether a repair makes sense.

Use each illustration with the table immediately beside it: match the callout to the component description, then read its material. The front and rear drawings have separate callout keys. This guide explains the material families and repair-planning decisions; the linked Plastic Repairs general procedure provides the repair and refinishing sequences.

items.name: Read the required safety references
items.detail: Before beginning service, review Safety Warnings in section 100-00 General Information and [Health and Safety Precautions](#/document/G1693189). That reference also requires review of Body Repair Health and Safety and General Precautions (100-00 General Information, Description and Operation) before body repair. Keep that additional referral as a prerequisite; its detailed precautions are outside this overview. Failure to follow the required safety instructions may result in serious personal injury.

items.name: Prevent unexpected starting
items.detail: Before inspection or service around or underneath the vehicle, disable remote start if equipped through the Central Display at Vehicle settings > Remote Start Setup. Otherwise the vehicle could be remotely started at any time, causing personal injury or death. Then switch the ignition OFF and remove the key from the vehicle to prevent another person from starting the engine during service; an accidental start may cause serious personal injury.

items.name: Protect eyes, ears and hands
items.detail: Wear eye and ear protection when servicing the vehicle. Wear protective gloves when handling pointed or sharp-edged components. Failure to follow these precautions may result in serious personal injury.

items.name: Handle repair chemicals safely
items.detail: Consult the material safety information sheet before using any specified cleaner, adhesive, filler or other repair material; improper use may present a health hazard and cause serious personal injury. Keep solvents away from ignition sources because they may ignite or explode, causing serious personal injury.

items.name: Identify the material and repair system
items.detail: Look for a moulded or stamped material designation, and establish whether the surface is grained or smooth before choosing preparation products. Use the matching branch of [Plastic Repairs](#/document/G1687510), including its equipment and materials tables. Follow the material-specific manufacturer’s label directions for repair materials, fillers and bonding agents; adhesive and patch systems can require different methods.

items.name: Keep the panel aligned
items.detail: When possible, carry out as much repair as possible with the component mounted on the vehicle. Its mountings hold it in the correct alignment; repairing it off the vehicle can introduce misalignment and cause the repair to fail. Structural cracks and large gouges require assessment for reinforcement; cosmetic damage may not need reinforcing cloth.

items.name: Start clean, dry and at room temperature
items.detail: Before repair, the panel should be dry and at 18 C (64.4 F) to 24 C (75.2 F). Thoroughly clean both sides before sanding or grinding. For Sheet-Molded Composite (SMC), first cover the break on both faces with masking tape, then clean the surrounding areas with plastics wax and grease remover. The tape prevents preparation cleaner from wicking through exposed fibers into the panel.

items.name: Prevent absorbed cleaner from spoiling the repair
items.detail: Never apply solvents such as lacquer thinner or reducer at any stage of plastic repair. Many plastics and reinforcing glass fibers absorb solvents, cleaners and water; swelling can then cause repair failure. Remove cleaners and water quickly, using air and heat to speed drying. Apply heat carefully because thermoplastics soften and can lose their shape.

items.name: Prepare bare plastic for adhesion
items.detail: Many plastics, particularly polyolefins, require plastics adhesion promoter on the substrate so repair materials and paint can bond. Apply it according to the product directions, and reapply whenever sanding or grinding exposes bare plastic through sealer or primer.

items.name: Preserve texture during refinishing
items.detail: For an approved refinish of a grained component, use only a gray scuff pad for light sanding; more aggressive sanding can flatten the grain. This refinishing precaution does not make a textured component repairable.

items.name: Match cleaning and paint to the selected system
items.detail: For refinishing, choose the correct cleaner for the solvent-based or water-based paint system. Clean with warm water and mild detergent, then plastic cleaner, and do not leave the part wet for extended periods. Water beading indicates that manufacturing release agents remain and further cleaning is needed. Follow the linked refinishing branch and Ford-approved paint-system instructions, including any required sealer and the paint manufacturer’s flex-additive recommendation. Refinish flexible and non-flexible components separately.

edits.text: Know the Plastic Before Repair
edits.why: Material, trim and surface finish determine whether the proposed repair is suitable.

edits.text: Check the actual vehicle’s trim before judging whether a plastic component can be repaired. These illustrations do not cover every available trim level, and that difference can change repair suitability. Components with moulded-in color or a textured finish are typically not considered repairable.
edits.why: A matching outline in a drawing does not guarantee a matching finish or a repairable surface. I make this check before choosing products or committing to a repair.

edits.text: Front Exterior Plastics
edits.why: Match each leader line to the adjoining front-component table. The branched hood leader points to the matching inserts on both sides; it does not identify the whole hood.

edits.text: Rear Exterior Plastics
edits.why: Use the rear drawing’s own table. Its leaders distinguish the trim around the luggage-compartment lid from the lower bumper area; the front drawing’s callout key does not apply here.

edits.text: Deciding Whether Repair Makes Sense
Before choosing a plastic repair, weigh the damage, access, replacement availability, cost, turnaround time and achievable quality:
edits.why: The aim is a sound result with the right appearance and fit, rather than simply proving that adhesive can fill the damage.

edits.text: Determine whether the damage is cosmetic or structural.
edits.why: The distinction helps determine the repair approach. The linked general procedure addresses structural cracks and large gouges; cosmetic damage may not require reinforcing cloth.

edits.text: Establish whether the repair can be carried out with the component on the vehicle.
edits.why: The vehicle’s mountings help maintain alignment during repair. Off-vehicle misalignment can undermine the finished repair and lead to failure.

edits.text: Check whether a replacement component is readily available.
edits.why: Replacement availability belongs in the decision alongside repair time and the quality that can be achieved.

edits.text: Compare the cost of repairing the component with the cost of replacement.
edits.why: Include repair labor and materials, and assess whether the damaged part can economically regain its original strength and appearance.

edits.text: Assess whether repair offers the fastest route to the highest-quality result.
edits.why: Judge speed together with appearance, fit and durability. A quick patch that cannot meet those needs is a poor repair choice.

edits.text: Automotive plastics come in many formulations, but they fall into 2 primary categories: thermoplastics and thermosetting plastics.
edits.why: Their response to heat explains an important repair difference: thermoplastics can be reshaped by reheating, while a thermosetting resin’s cure is irreversible.

edits.text: Thermosetting Plastics: An Irreversible Cure
Thermosetting plastics are generally made from 2-part thermosetting resins. Mixing the parts generates heat and produces an irreversible cure. Repair therefore requires a 2-part adhesive.
edits.why: I think of the cure like baking a cake: warming it again will not put the ingredients back in the bowl. That is why remoulding by reheating is not the repair route described here.

edits.text: A reinforced example is Sheet-Molded Composite (SMC):
Sheet-Molded Composite (SMC) combines glass fibers or nylon fibers with thermosetting polyester resins. Once fully cured, the resulting material is strong and rigid.
edits.why: The fibers reinforce the cured resin. During repair preparation, exposed fibers can also wick cleaner into the damaged panel, which explains the masking precaution in the linked repair procedure. One list in the linked repair procedure puts SMC among thermoplastics, but its own later explanation and this overview describe thermosetting material. I follow that thermosetting classification here; [SMC manufacturer IDI Composites](https://www.idicomposites.com/product/smc-bmc/) also identifies its SMC as a thermoset composite. That classification does not replace the component-specific repair instructions.

edits.text: Sheet-Molded Composite (SMC) resembles fiberglass but is not identical to it. Ford Motor Company uses Sheet-Molded Composite (SMC) in components such as fenders, hoods and liftgates.
edits.why: These are examples of Ford applications, not a declaration that every Mustang panel in those locations uses this material. Identify the actual component before selecting its repair method.

edits.text: Thermoplastics: Reshaping with Heat

Thermoplastic compounds are formed through a reversible process, so reheating can remould them repeatedly. This makes plastic welding a possible repair alternative. They can also be repaired with a 2-part adhesive and filler materials, using reinforcement where needed. Common applications include interior trim, wheel flares, body side cladding and bumper covers.
edits.why: Heat can help reshape this material, but the same softening can let a component lose its intended shape. Welding is a possibility to evaluate after identification, not an automatic choice for every thermoplastic repair.

edits.text: Polyolefins: Pay Attention to Adhesion

Polyolefins belong to the thermoplastic family and have a characteristic oily or waxy feel when sanded or ground. They respond well to remoulding with heat, making plastic welding a possible repair method. Most adhesive repair materials and paint will not bond to exposed raw polyolefin unless an adhesion promoter formulated for plastic is applied first. Otherwise, their repair follows the same principles as other thermoplastics. Applications include bumper covers, fan shrouds and wheel housings.
edits.why: A neat-looking patch still needs a dependable bond underneath it. The promoter prepares the raw surface for adhesion; if sanding exposes it again, the preparation must be restored before continuing.

edits.text: Identify the plastic correctly before selecting a repair method; that choice is essential to a high-quality result. Continue with [Plastic Repairs](#/document/G1687510) (501-25 Body Repairs - General Information, General Procedures) for the applicable identification, repair or refinishing sequence.
edits.why: This overview helps choose the appropriate path. The linked procedure separates composite-panel repairs, thermoplastic repairs, tab repairs and refinishing, and retains the material manufacturer’s instructions for the selected system.

readerOutcome: Understand component maps, repair-versus-replacement factors and material families, with an explicit source classification conflict disclosure. This is preparation and orientation, not the full linked repair procedure.
teachingNotes: Every requested primary text block is rewritten under its original block ID; headings remain concise single-line titles.
Primary tables and illustrations remain separate and unchanged. The prose explains navigation without reproducing their material assignments.
The irreversible-cure analogy explains thermosetting behavior, while the thermoplastic discussion connects useful heat response with the risk of losing shape.

Supporting evidence supplies applicable startup, personal protection, chemical handling, alignment, cleaning, temperature and adhesion precautions. Unrelated lifting, heavy-assembly and power-running-board instructions are excluded.
The supporting tab illustration shows repair areas around a generic bumper opening. It supplies no removal or refit sequence, and none is inferred or taught here.
The mandatory nested Body Repair Health and Safety and General Precautions referral is retained by title without inventing an unavailable document link.
This remains an overview with a required referral for repair execution; supporting material tests and detailed repair sequences are not presented as a standalone workshop procedure.

SMC & BMC
We perfect the chemistry. You perfect the process.
About SMC & BMC
At IDI, we manufacture Sheet Molding Compound (SMC) and Bulk Molding Compound (BMC), two highly engineered thermoset composite materials that deliver strength, durability, and design flexibility across a wide range of industries.
SMC & BMC are mixtures of polymer resin, inert fillers, fiber reinforcement, catalysts, pigments & stabilizers, release agents, and thickeners. 
While SMC and BMC share similar underlying chemistries, each is uniquely processed and optimized to meet different manufacturing methods, performance requirements, and end-use applications.
SMC and BMC are sold by IDI in an 
uncured
 state. This means that they are ready to be formed into finished parts through the application of heat and pressure.
How it's made
Sheet Molding Compound (SMC)
SMC is made through a continuous, controlled process that combines resin and filler with a glass reinforcement. The paste is spread uniformly onto a bottom film and chopped glass fibers are randomly deposited onto the paste. A second paste is introduced to the top of the glass chop where a second film is also introduced to sandwich the two paste sides with the glass fiber. There is pressure applied to get the sheet to a predetermined thickness. The material then goes to a maturation room for a period of time to reach optimal viscosity. 
Where performance meets possibility.
Whether you're engineering a Class A automotive component, designing products for a new residential or commercial build, specifying high-strength materials for infrastructure applications, or developing electrical components that demand exceptional insulation and performance, SMC delivers.
Why choose SMC?
SMC’s unique combination of strength, lightweight performance, design flexibility, and customizable formulations makes it the material of choice across a wide range of industries. No matter the application, SMC is engineered to help manufacturers achieve better performance, greater efficiency, and lasting durability.
 Easily molded into complex geometries 
 Excellent mechanical properties 
 Electrical insulation 
 Superior surface appearance 
 High strength 
How it's made
Bulk Molding Compound (BMC)
BMC is made through a batch mixing process that combines resin and filler with a glass reinforcement. Bulk Molding Compound (BMC) is highly filled and reinforced with short fibers. Glass reinforcement represents between 10% and 30%, with glass length typically between 1/32-inch and 1/2-inch. The end result is a dough-like compound. 
Powering precision across industries.
BMC is the material of choice whether you're manufacturing intricate electrical components, high-volume industrial parts, durable consumer products, or precision-molded components that demand exceptional dimensional stability and electrical performance. 
Why choose BMC?
BMC is a reliable material that provides excellent electrical insulation, heat resistance, and mechanical strength. This makes BMC the material of choice for manufacturers seeking reliable performance and efficient production.
 Superior flame & track resistance 
 Electrical insulation properties 
 Corrosion & stain resistance 
 Color stability 
 Low shrink
